Syllables are either CV or V, with syllabic nasals functioning as V syllables, and stress is predictable, with primary stress on the penultimate syllable, secondary stress on the first syllable of words of four or more syllables and light stress on the fourth syllable of seven syllable words and the fourth and sixth syllables of eight syllable words.

The note begins on printed p.…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is fully predictable: primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word. All syllables are CV or V (syllabic nasals count as V), so there is no weight sensitivity to invoke.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress on the first syllable of words of four or more syllables; an additional 'light' stress on the 4th syllable of 7-syllable words and on the 4th and 6th syllables of 8-syllable words (i.e., a left-edge secondary plus alternating lighter beats in long words).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; stress described as 'predictable'. Same note reports two vowel phonemes (/i/,/u/ and /e/,/o/,/a/ series) with stressed vs unstressed allophones, which corroborates that stress is a real word-level property.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level ('words of four or more syllables'); stated in a footnote on the practical orthography of the language, in a Bislama-Tangoan comparative paper, by a missionary-linguist resident at Tangoa (Camden, Bible translator, author of the 1977 Bislama dictionary). Not a dedicated phonology; no instrumental data. The statement was verified against the page scan, not only the scanned.
new_statements.identity_note: Camden 1979 describes "Tangoan, the language spoken on Tangoa, a small island off the south coast of Santo" (p. 53) = Glottolog tang1347 (Glottolog's name "Movono"; aliases Tangoa, Santo). Camden notes a prestige "true Tangoan" register with apico-labial phonemes used by men; the stress rule is stated for the language as a whole. Caution on one Glottolog reference: Gordon 1889 "Sketch of the Santo grammar" describes a WEST-Santo variety (Wulua/Valpay dialects; Macdonald's preface says "a language or dialect spoken on the west side of the island"), not Tangoa.

sources.citation: Annand, J. 1891. A grammar of the Tangoan-Santo language. In D. Macdonald (ed.), South Sea Languages vol. II, 1-14. Melbourne: Melbourne Public Library.
sources.note: Alphabet note (p. 1): vowels a e i o u, diphthongs ai au oi ao (au, oi long and short), consonant remarks incl. the interdental-labial t; no statement on accent or stress. The volume's 'accent' remarks belong to the Malekula (Morton), Baki and Bierian grammars, not to Annand's Tangoan.

tone.quote: STRESS PATTERNS. Stress was found to be predictable, primary stress occurring on the penultimate syllable, and secondary stress occurring on the first syllable of words of more than three syllables. In the simplest material, all syllables consist of a consonant followed by a vowel. Words of one such syllable carry stress. The shift of stress is shown in the following series. [...] Sequences of vowels were found to behave analogously, the first vowel of the series forming a syllable with the preceeding consonant, and each succeeding vowel being syllabic, taking stress or otherwise according to the pattern outlined.
